source.title: Tilted Sharpness-Aware Minimization
source.authors: Tian Li; Tianyi Zhou; Jeff A. Bilmes

record.file_problem: The supplied text appears to contain the full paper, including appendices. No garbling or cutoff noted.
record.tranche_reason: Tests a new optimizer on image and text tasks and reports test performance and sharpness compared with ERM and SAM. It does not test the claim versions’ specified settings or measures.
record.gate_note: The paper compares TSAM, ERM, and SAM on test performance and neighborhood sharpness. It does not test random-label memorization, width sweeps, convolutional versus fully connected networks, adaptive optimizers, batch size, dropout, magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, or removal of memorized examples.
record.test_reason: The study uses the premise that flatter minima can improve generalization to develop TSAM and evaluates its performance. It tests none of V1–V8. In particular, its Gaussian neighborhood-loss statistics and Hessian eigenvalues do not measure V7's magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance or compare its ranking of generalization gaps against other measures.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors' conclusion: bounded-tilt TSAM is smoother than SAM, increasing tilt favors flatter solutions under their theoretical assumptions, and their experiments favor TSAM. Their claim of consistent superiority is broader than the tables justify: individual GLUE metrics and some image comparisons with SAM variants do not favor TSAM. They explicitly leave a rigorous account of the flatness–generalization relationship open.
record.recipe_differences: Introduces TSAM, an exponentially tilted neighborhood-loss objective and approximate HMC-inspired sampler; compares it with ERM, SAM, and SAM variants. It does not reproduce the original studies’ interventions or measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Tilt t, number of sampled perturbations s, perturbation radius ρ, dataset, model, objective, and evaluation metric; the paper reports that test performance varies with t and that scheduling t showed no significant difference from fixed t on noisy CIFAR100.

fits_no_version.finding: TSAM improves reported image test accuracy over ERM and vanilla SAM in the extracted settings and improves the reported GLUE average, although it does not win every task or every comparison with SAM variants.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Tuned TSAM can improve held-out performance over ERM and vanilla SAM on the tested image and GLUE workloads.

fits_no_version.finding: For ResNet18 on CIFAR100, TSAM produces smaller Gaussian neighborhood-loss mean and variance and smaller leading Hessian eigenvalues. Its ordinary training loss is higher and ordinary test loss lower than ERM's and SAM's.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this optimizer comparison, flatter solutions under unscaled neighborhood and Hessian measures accompany better test loss; this does not establish V7's magnitude-aware generalization-gap ranking.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning; Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: The text says the practical sampler does not guarantee a consistent estimator of the TSAM integral. Generalization-versus-flatness understanding is acknowledged as open. Table 1's flattened GLUE layout makes the CoLA TSAM value unassignable here; parenthetical values in several accuracy cells are not defined in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1's additional SAM variants (ESAM1, ESAM2, PGN, RSAM) and the remaining GLUE comparator values were not extracted as separate rows; rows prioritize ERM/SAM/TSAM comparisons. Additional convergence plots and hyperparameter figures are figure-only and were not transcribed as rows.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fitting of fixed random labels alongside natural-label generalization, with random-label held-out accuracy at chance.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of learned or imposed local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizers under limited or broader tuning. The study explicitly uses no adaptivity.
Batch-size effects and compensating training recipes. Batch size is fixed at 64.
Dropout interventions, dataset-size dependence and interaction with augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with training–test error gaps, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equal-sized random removals and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels apply because none of the specified versions is tested. Table 3's corrected ordinary test losses are 0.9302, 0.7414 and 0.7163 for ERM, SAM and TSAM; these do not turn the study into a test of V7's specified measure.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or natural-label versus random-label comparison.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold analysis.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected architectures.
Measures neighborhood loss mean and variance and Hessian eigenvalues, but not magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or its ranking of training-test gaps across networks.
No removal of memorized training examples.
